clinicalPearls: The commonest inherited macular dystrophy, usually autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic variants in ABCA4
Typically presents in childhood or young adulthood with progressive bilateral central visual loss and difficulty reading
Yellow-white pisciform (fish-tail) flecks at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium around the macula and posterior pole are characteristic
A macular atrophic 'beaten-bronze' appearance develops, and vision may be reduced before obvious fundus change
A dark or 'silent' choroid on fluorescein angiography, from lipofuscin masking, is a classic sign
Autofluorescence imaging highlights flecks and atrophy and is useful for monitoring progression
Patients should avoid high-dose vitamin A supplementation, which may accelerate lipofuscin accumulation
reference.pathophysiology: Stargardt disease is caused by defects in ABCA4, a transporter in photoreceptor outer-segment discs that clears retinoid by-products of the visual cycle. Loss of transporter function allows toxic bisretinoid compounds to accumulate and form excessive lipofuscin (including A2E) within the retinal pigment epithelium. This lipofuscin overload is cytotoxic to the retinal pigment epithelium, leading to its dysfunction and death and secondary loss of the overlying photoreceptors, concentrated at the macula. The result is progressive central photoreceptor and pigment-epithelial atrophy with the characteristic flecks representing lipofuscin-laden cells.
additionalDifferentials: Pattern dystrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium
additionalInvestigations: Fundus autofluorescence imaging to characterise flecks and map atrophy
Optical coherence tomography to assess photoreceptor and pigment-epithelial loss
Fluorescein angiography demonstrating the dark/silent choroid
Electroretinography and electrooculography to assess extent of retinal dysfunction
Colour vision testing and formal visual acuity assessment
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric visual decline prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Widespread (rather than macular) retinal dysfunction on ERG indicating a poorer-prognosis phenotype
Inadvertent high-dose vitamin A intake potentially accelerating disease
reference.prognosis: Central vision is progressively lost, often to the level of legal blindness, while peripheral vision is usually preserved; the rate of progression varies with genotype and age of onset, and gene- and pharmacologically-targeted therapies are under active investigation.
pitfalls: Labelling early cases as functional or refractive when acuity loss precedes visible fundus change
Recommending or overlooking high-dose vitamin A supplements that may worsen the disease
Confusing it with age-related macular degeneration in older patients and mismanaging accordingly
Failing to arrange genetic testing and counselling for recessive inheritance
management: No established disease-modifying therapy; management centres on low-vision rehabilitation with magnifiers and visual aids to maximise remaining vision
Advise avoidance of high-dose vitamin A supplementation, which may accelerate toxic lipofuscin (A2E) accumulation
Ultraviolet and blue-light protection with sunglasses to limit photic retinal injury
Monitor progression with fundus autofluorescence and optical coherence tomography
Provide educational, occupational and visual-impairment registration support
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive ABCA4 disorder, with discussion of emerging gene- and drug-directed therapies and clinical trials
